options.option_text: Random in order
Arranged in order of time
Painted in colour
Repeated in cycles

questions.explanation: Gk. 'chronos' = time. Same root: chronic (long-lasting), chronicle (record of events), anachronism (out of time), synchronous (at the same time).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A modern invention
Something out of its correct historical period
A very old object
A confusing statement

questions.explanation: Gk. 'ana-' (against, up) + 'chronos' (time) = against-time. Example: a wristwatch in a Roman-era film is an anachronism.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A conversation between two
A long speech by one person
A set of musical notes
A formal letter

questions.explanation: Gk. 'monos' (one) + 'logos' (speech). Contrast with 'dialogue' (di- = two; 'two speaking'). Also 'soliloquy' — a monologue spoken to oneself.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Occurring at different times
Occurring at the same time
Very close in distance
Repeating at fixed intervals

questions.explanation: Gk. 'syn-' (together) + 'chronos' (time). Opposite is asynchronous. Tech context: 'synchronous communication' = participants online simultaneously.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A curse on the dead
A speech of praise, especially for the dead
A medical examination
An official investigation

questions.explanation: Gk. 'eu-' (good) + 'logos' (word) = 'good words'. Delivered at funerals. Antonym: 'diatribe' / 'invective' (bitter speech).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Sudden and severe
Long-lasting, persisting over time
Contagious
Uncurable

questions.explanation: Gk. 'chronikos' = relating to time. Antonym in medicine: acute (sudden, short-term, severe).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A preface at the start
A concluding section at the end
A dedication to a person
A dramatic break in a play

questions.explanation: Gk. 'epi-' (upon, after) + 'logos' (word). Opposite of 'prologue' (pro- = before). Often used in books and plays.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A traditional saying
A newly coined word or expression
A biological term
A formal argument

questions.stem: In documentary film-making, a 'travelogue' is best described as which of the following?

options.option_text: a scientific study of human migration patterns
a film or written account of journeys and travels
a formal debate between two seasoned travellers
a catalogue of geographic landmarks across nations

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'travelogue' = travel + -logue (account/narrative), so it is a recorded narrative of travel experiences. Option A confuses it with demography/migration studies; Option D misapplies 'catalogue', which means a systematic list, not a travel record.

questions.stem: A 'chronometer' was historically prized by naval navigators primarily because it could do what?

options.option_text: measure ocean depths and underwater distances
keep highly accurate time even on rough open seas
record the biological age of marine organisms reliably
track the velocity of celestial bodies at night

questions.explanation: B is correct: CHRON (time) + METER (measure) = instrument for measuring time precisely. Accurate timekeeping at sea allowed sailors to calculate longitude. Option C wrongly links CHRON to biology; Option A invents a nautical function not suggested by the root.

questions.stem: A historian conducting a 'diachronic' study of the Hindi language is examining which of the following?

options.option_text: dialectal variations existing simultaneously across regions
phonetic patterns found in present-day spoken Hindi only
how Hindi has evolved and changed across historical time
logical contradictions present in modern Hindi grammar rules

questions.explanation: C is correct: DIA (through/across) + CHRON (time) = through time, so diachronic analysis tracks language change over history. Option A describes 'synchronic' analysis (same time, different places), the classic confusion point tested in linguistics exams.

questions.stem: The 'Decalogue', a term derived from Greek DECA (ten) + LOGOS (word), refers to which of the following?

options.option_text: a ten-day sermon series delivered by the prophet Moses
the Ten Commandments recorded in Exodus and Deuteronomy
a twelve-part chronicle of ancient Near-Eastern kingdoms
a formal catalogue listing the ten canonical law codes

questions.explanation: B is correct: DECA (ten) + LOGUE (words/utterances) = the ten utterances/commandments. Option A introduces 'ten-day sermon' which is a plausible distractor but misreads DECA as a duration rather than a count; Option C uses 'twelve', misapplying DECA entirely.

questions.stem: A 'chronograph', found on aviation watches and racing instruments, primarily serves which function?

options.option_text: displays the current time across two separate time zones
functions as a stopwatch to measure and record elapsed time
uses atomic resonance oscillation for absolute timekeeping
adjusts its display automatically for daylight saving changes

questions.explanation: B is correct: CHRON (time) + GRAPH (write/record) = a device that records time intervals, i.e., a stopwatch mechanism. Option C describes an atomic clock, a different instrument; Option A describes a dual-timezone watch, which is a 'GMT' or 'world-time' complication.

questions.stem: In physics, a pendulum is called 'isochronous' when which specific property holds true for its motion?

options.option_text: its amplitude gradually increases over successive oscillations
its time period stays equal regardless of swing amplitude
it synchronises automatically with an external magnetic field
its period depends entirely on ambient temperature changes

questions.explanation: B is correct: ISO (equal) + CHRON (time) + OUS = having equal time periods. For small angles, a simple pendulum is approximately isochronous — its period is independent of amplitude. Option C confuses 'iso' with 'syn' (together); Option D describes temperature-compensated clocks, a different concept.

questions.stem: When Cardinal Newman wrote his 'Apologia Pro Vita Sua', the word 'apologia' (APO + LOGIA) carried which precise meaning?

options.option_text: a sincere verbal apology for specific past wrongdoings made
a formal written defence of one's own beliefs and conduct
a brief introductory preface attached to a scholarly work
a critical analysis that highlights an opponent's weaknesses

questions.explanation: B is correct: APO (away from, in defence) + LOGIA (reasoned speech/account) = a formal defence/justification. This is its classical Greek rhetorical sense, distinct from the modern 'apology' (expressing regret). Option A is the trap: modern English 'apology' has shifted to mean regret, but 'apologia' retains the original defensive-speech meaning.
